recommendations.name: Marcia Suzuki
recommendations.title: Chair, Shema Bible Translation; International Dean, College of Applied Linguistics and Languages, University of the Nations
recommendations.org: Leads the OBT Lab, Kansas City
recommendations.snippet: To make resources people can trust, we must guide AI through the same careful steps scholars have always followed. … This takes deep knowledge of the Bible, of language, and of AI. Josh has all three. … That combination is rare.
full: Hello, this is Marcia Suzuki. I chair Shema Bible Translation, and I serve as International Dean of the College of Applied Linguistics and Languages at the University of the Nations. I also lead the OBT Lab in Kansas City. There we develop AI tools for oral Bible translation.
I am glad to recommend Josh Frost and the work he is doing.

Josh and his wife, Katie, spent a week with our team in Kansas City. Their expertise in linguistics, biblical languages and oral Bible translation helped us refine the tools and resources we are developing here at the OBT lab, such as Meaning Maps for Bible translation and agentic AI tools to help translators internalize and translate the Bible into their mother tongues. We were so impressed that we decided to work together as formal partners.

For more than thirty years, I have worked with indigenous peoples in Brazil. I have seen the same need again and again. Translators and pastors in these communities do not have the tools we take for granted. In English, we have commentaries, Bible dictionaries, and grammars on our shelves. Most minority-language translators have none of these in a language they understand well. They do serious work with very little support.

It is no wonder. Experts spend hundreds, or even thousands, of hours doing repetitive work to make trustworthy dictionaries, encyclopedias, and commentaries, in a single language. Thousands of scholars have spent their lives making the resources we have in English.
Making the same resources in the 50 most spoken languages of the world would take thousands of people to do the traditional route.

AI can help change this. But it is not as simple as asking a chatbot a question. To make resources people can trust, we must guide AI through the same careful steps scholars have always followed. That means close study of the original languages. It means attention to context. It means checking against good scholarship, and review by people who know the field. This takes deep knowledge of the Bible, of language, and of AI.

Josh has all three. He is trained in linguistics and classical languages. He understands translation from the inside. And he knows how to make AI do careful, disciplined work. That combination is rare.
The system Josh is building combines his unique skill set into something truly remarkable. What used to take hundreds of hours can now take a fraction of the time and still be as trustworthy.

If this work succeeds, translators and pastors in many languages will finally have the resources they need. Their translations will be stronger. Their teaching will be more faithful. I believe this is a wise investment, and I am happy to support it.

recommendations.name: Swapna Alexander
recommendations.title: Lead Bible Translation Consultant
recommendations.snippet: Making trustworthy, OBT-specific exegetical resources available in majority languages would have a significant impact. … I believe resources of this kind could fill an important gap for the growing OBT movement and equip translators to engage Scripture more deeply in languages that are genuinely accessible to them.
full: Exegetical resources are essential for Bible translators because good translation begins with a sound understanding of Scripture—its meaning, context, discourse, culture, and emotional dynamics. This is particularly important in Oral Bible Translation (OBT), where meaning is communicated not only through words but also through performance features such as intonation, emphasis, pace, and emotion.

At the same time, there remains a significant gap in exegetical resources designed specifically for OBT translators. Many existing resources are written, academically oriented, and primarily available in English. For translators who work orally or rely on a language of wider communication other than English, access to appropriate resources can therefore be very limited.

I have known Joshua Frost for more than four years and have observed his work with OBT practitioners in different cultural and linguistic settings. Joshua has done extensive research in emotion exegesis and in the particular exegetical needs of oral translation. His work recognizes that emotions are integral to meaning and that translators need to understand the biblical context, relationships, expectations, values, and cultural dynamics behind a passage so that both the wording and performance of an oral translation are faithful. Just as importantly, Joshua has consistently sought ways to make rigorous research practical and accessible to translators rather than leaving it at the academic level.

Making trustworthy, OBT-specific exegetical resources available in majority languages would have a significant impact. It would give many more mother-tongue translators direct access to the biblical and cultural background they need, strengthen internalization and drafting, support more informed translation decisions, and ultimately contribute to clearer, more accurate, natural, and engaging oral translations. I believe resources of this kind could fill an important gap for the growing OBT movement and equip translators to engage Scripture more deeply in languages that are genuinely accessible to them.
I am grateful for the research and resource development Joshua is investing in this important area and believe it has the potential to serve OBT teams around the world.
